description: Hello, as the "El Sagan Bumbastico" team, we are looking for teammates with software and presentation skills who are compatible with teamwork to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our hope is to run toward great achievements together and reach the Global Finals.
summary:
We built Canola Atlas for farmers who want to grow canola but don't know where to start. NASA has years of satellite and climate data that could answer most of their questions, but a farmer in Tekirdağ or Şanlıurfa isn't going to read a soil moisture chart. So we tried to turn that data into answers they can use: is my field suitable, is there frost tonight, and is it too soon to plant canola here again?

The app pulls climate data from NASA POWER, crop health from MODIS, rainfall from GPM, soil moisture from SMAP and imagery from Landsat and Sentinel-2. A farmer draws their field on the map and gets short daily warnings, a crop health score and a rotation check that flags blackleg and clubroot risk. We also scored all 972 districts of Türkiye for winter and spring canola.

Our assistant CanolSI explains everything in plain Turkish, and farmers can learn from each other in Social Field. Better rotation decisions mean less disease, steadier yields and more homegrown vegetable oil.
details:
Why we built it

Canola is one of the best crops a farmer in Türkiye can add to a wheat rotation. It breaks disease cycles, it's in demand, and the country still imports a large share of its vegetable oil. But most farmers who try it for the first time are guessing. They don't know if their land suits it, when to sow, or how long to wait before planting it on the same field again. Getting that last one wrong lets blackleg build up in the soil, and the damage can last for years.

NASA already collects most of the data needed to answer these questions. The problem is that it's spread across different portals and written for scientists. We wanted to put it in a farmer's pocket and make it say something simple.

How it works

The farmer picks their province, district and village, then draws the field boundary with a finger on a satellite map. After that they enter which crops they've grown in recent years and when they sowed. From there the app does the rest:

• Today in the field: a few short lines about frost, rain, wind and whether it's a good time to spray.

• Crop health: a single percentage based on MODIS vegetation data, with map layers for NDVI, land surface temperature, GPM rainfall, SMAP soil moisture and Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery.

• Rotation check: how long it has been since canola or another brassica was on the field, and a clear warning if it's too soon.

• Suitability: a score for winter and spring canola on the farmer's own field, plus a map of every district in Türkiye with country, province and district reports.

• Weather and soil: past years and soil properties shown as plain lines, each marked suitable, caution or not suitable.

• CanoSI: our assistant. Farmers can ask it anything in their own words, and it answers using their field's data.

• Social Field: a place for farmers to share what's working, with a short video feed in the style of Reels for quick lessons on sowing, pests and harvest.

How we calculate suitability

We split Türkiye into 6,682 cells of roughly 11 km. For each cell we take climate values from NASA POWER: January temperature, the coldest night, temperature during flowering, rainfall and soil wetness. We adjust temperature for elevation, then add soil pH and clay from ISRIC SoilGrids. Each value is checked against FAO's requirements for canola (Brassica napus). The weakest factor limits the final score, because a plant can't make up for a killing frost with good soil. District scores are the average of the cells inside them.

What it means for farmers

• A beginner can make a reasonable decision without reading a single chart.

• Longer gaps between canola crops mean less disease and fewer chemical treatments.

• The district map shows where canola could grow but isn't grown yet, which matters for a country trying to produce more of its own oil.

What we used

The app is written in HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with Leaflet for the maps. On Android it runs inside a small Java app. Firebase handles accounts, the social feed and security, and CanoSI runs on Google Gemini through Firebase AI Logic. We prepared the district grid in Python with Shapely, using OpenStreetMap boundaries. Besides NASA, we use Open-Meteo for forecasts and elevation, ISRIC SoilGrids for soil, and FAO Ecocrop for crop thresholds.

What makes it different

Most farm apps show weather. We focused on the decision a farmer actually has to make: should I plant canola on this field this season? To answer that we bring together rotation history, disease risk and NASA data in one place. The district atlas and the video feed came from asking what a first-time canola farmer would really open the app for.

What we kept in mind

• Keep it simple. Short Turkish sentences, one decision per screen, no jargon.

• Be honest about the limits. The suitability map is a regional guide at about 11 km, not a promise for a single field. When a farmer enters a soil lab result, the app uses it instead of the satellite estimate.

• We haven't tested it in the field yet. When we compared our map with a published canola suitability map from Atatürk University, the results matched in the Aegean, Marmara, Mediterranean and inland regions, but differed in Thrace and the Southeast. We're working on that. Next we want to compare it with official planting statistics, get an agronomist to review it, and test it with local growers.
